Man in Brooklyn Jail Helped Direct Iranian Terror Plot Against U.S. Bombers in Britain

Federal prosecutors say an Iran-linked militant already locked up in a Brooklyn jail continued coordinating terrorist operations through coded phone calls to his family in Iraq.

Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood Al-Saadi, an Iranian-Iraqi national, used calls to his mother and sister to pass instructions and arrange payments for an attack on RAF Fairford, a British airbase used by American B-1 bombers.

According to the indictment:

The suspects allegedly planned to attack the base using 3 vans disguised as commercial vehicles, including fuel delivery and swimming pool service vans.

The vehicles were prepared with fuel barrels, chemical accelerants and metal objects intended to increase casualties.

The group paid operatives to film and surveil the base in August 2026.

On September 24, Al-Saadi told relatives to pass along money, saying, “give him money so we can do it.”

On September 26, the vans approached the base. At least 2 were stopped at a security checkpoint, and British authorities arrested suspects the following morning.

Prosecutors also charged Mohsen Mohajeri, an IRGC operative, and Mohammad Ali Al-Hassani, who directed the operation from Iran.

The failed attack was allegedly part of a wider Iranian-linked campaign involving nearly 20 attacks and attempted attacks against Jewish institutions, Israeli interests and other targets across Europe and the U.S.

Al-Saadi was already being held in Brooklyn on separate terrorism charges. The new allegations raise questions about how a detainee could allegedly continue coordinating an overseas attack from a U.S. federal jail.

Iran denies involvement.

If people across the country trade the same contract on the same exchange, regulators should be able to see the whole market.

A single federal rulebook gives the CFTC a clearer view of trading activity across state lines and gives exchanges a consistent standard to follow. 

Why is that important?

For traders, that means the same protections wherever they trade. For new exchanges, it lowers the cost of competing nationwide.

Let me briefly sum up where we are with AI.

Everyone can feel it and everyone can see it. I believe 2026 is the turning point. We see major advances every day, but with all the excitement about the latest benchmarks, it’s easy to lose sight of the bigger picture.

Anthropic has just released Claude Fable 5.2, its latest flagship model. It’s outstanding. Anyone who has tested it knows how good it is, and in its blog posts, Anthropic has also highlighted advances beyond coding: new findings in physics and hardware design, as well as a method for predicting viral protein structures developed with Mythos 5.2.

Fable 5.2 even built an operating system prototype by coordinating more than 1,000 subagents over eight days. At the same time, Anthropic acknowledged in its system card that it has a separate, unreleased research model that is somewhat more capable than Mythos 5.2. This could be “Model 4,” although that connection has not been confirmed.

Meanwhile, the competition isn’t slowing down. Google has caught up in a big way, and Gemini 4 Carbon is outstanding. Google also says it is using its own models for research and making new discoveries. Rumors suggest that a successor called Krypton is already being tested, though its capabilities remain unconfirmed.

Today, the authors of AI 2027 updated their prediction. The AI Futures Project now forecasts that AI capable of doing the work of a team of top human AI researchers will likely arrive in 2027, absent a major slowdown. They estimate that AI-driven acceleration of AI research is already five months ahead of their original scenario.

And we shouldn’t forget what AI systems have already achieved in mathematics. OpenAI says an internal system produced a solution to the Navier–Stokes Millennium Prize Problem. And this model is already outdated, as OpenAI said in their blogpost. 

What I’m trying to say is this: I regularly say that the takeoff began in 2026 and that 2027 will be a crazy year. Perhaps the craziest year in human history. But when we look back on this year, I think it will become clear just how crazy 2026 already was.

I’ve devoted myself to AI since GPT-3.5, and I now work full-time to make this technological revolution tangible. Just a few years ago, LLMs like GPT-4 seemed like stochastic parrots. They hallucinated and, compared with today’s models, felt like trivial machines. Of course, they were never actually trivial. But looking back, the pace of development since o1 in late 2024 has kept increasing, and now the sudden explosion in capabilities feels tangible.

So enjoy these last months of relative calm. I believe 2027 will be the year of superintelligence. And nothing will be the same again.

Official Statement from Al-Madrasatu Ar-Rahmaniyyah (AMAR) Regarding the Recent Podcast Trailer.

As-salāmu ʿalaykum wa raḥmatullāhi wa barakātuh,
Yesterday, a short trailer was published on the AMAR YouTube channel for an upcoming podcast on takfīrism, the Khawārij, and the origins of that group. The trailer, produced by our editing team, grouped together a number of names and figures, including Sayyid Quṭb, along with contemporary charitable organisations. It also used labels such as "Islamist" and "jihadist." In doing so, it made claims that had not been fact-checked or verified, and it associated people and organisations with one another in ways that were inaccurate and unjust.
When the trailer was released, I was travelling in East Africa for a dawrah ʿilmiyyah. I approved its publication, but I did not watch it properly in full beforehand. That was my mistake, and I take full responsibility for it. I sincerely apologise for the inaccurate information it contained, and to everyone who was offended, hurt, or wrongly associated by it.
I ask that I be held to what I said in the podcast itself. That is where I spoke on this subject from my own research and understanding, and anyone can watch it and judge it for themselves.
I never want to cause harm to any Muslim, or to be a means through which any Muslim is harmed. Nor do I wish to wrong anyone by attributing to them words or positions that are not theirs. This applies even to someone I disagree with, and even to someone I believe has erred.
Going forward, in shāʾ Allāh, all refutations, documentaries and similar content from AMAR will go through a proper editing, review and verification process before publication.
I ask Allah to forgive our shortcomings, and I kindly ask you to overlook this error.
Jazākumullāhu khayran.

Ustādh Abdulrahman Hassan CEO, Al-Madrasatu Ar-Rahmaniyyah (AMAR)

🇺🇸 Jensen Huang's scandal could trigger an AI meltdown, and a bigger war is brewing inside Washington

Economist Philip Pilkington believes the controversy is part of a much bigger battle over who controls the future of AI, and whether America should be competing with China or trying to shut it out.

And he suspects powerful interests are using it to settle that fight.

At the centre of the dispute is a fundamental disagreement over how America wins the AI race.

Jensen has argued that Nvidia should be allowed to sell advanced chips to China, maintaining its global market share and funding the next generation of technology.

But Philip says China hawks inside Washington want the opposite: tighter restrictions designed to keep Beijing behind.

Meanwhile, American AI companies are betting heavily on proprietary, closed-source models, while China is pursuing an increasingly open-source approach.

Philip believes Washington is backing the wrong strategy.

And the timing couldn't be worse.

A renewed U.S-China trade war could trigger Chinese restrictions on rare earth minerals, further pressure American technology companies and complicate Washington's position in the Middle East.

And Philip believes the wider AI market is already dangerously exposed.

And for Trump, the danger is that a fight intended to weaken China could end up damaging America's most important technology industry.
